title: Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band of Pottawatomi Indians v. Patchak
lead: David Patchak wanted to stop a tribal casino near his Michigan property. By the time his challenge reached the Supreme Court, the United States already held the casino site in trust, and the dispute was whether he could challenge that acquisition at all.

actors.name: Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band of Pottawatomi Indians
actors.role: Federally recognized tribe that requested the trust acquisition to develop a casino.

actors.name: David Patchak
actors.role: Nearby resident who challenged the acquisition without claiming any interest in the acquired land.

actors.name: Secretary of the Interior
actors.role: Federal official who approved and completed the acquisition.

actors.name: Michigan Gambling Opposition
actors.role: Organization that brought the earlier environmental and gaming challenge.

proceedings: The District Court dismissed on zone-of-interests grounds. The D.C. Circuit reversed and rejected an alternative immunity defense. The Supreme Court affirmed and remanded, leaving the acquisition’s statutory validity unresolved.
limits: This is the 2012 threshold decision, using the statute’s then-current numbering and the opinion’s standing terminology. It does not report later litigation, determine the Band’s status in 1934, or establish that the casino acquisition was unlawful.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A tribe seeks land for economic development
sections.cue: Why did the Band want the United States to acquire the Bradley Property?
paragraphs: The Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band of Pottawatomi Indians had a long history but obtained formal federal recognition in 1999. In 2001, the Band asked the Secretary of the Interior to acquire the Bradley Property in Wayland Township, Michigan, in trust under §5 of the Indian Reorganization Act, then codified at 25 U.S.C. §465. The Band planned gaming operations to support economic development, self-sufficiency, tribal government, and social and educational programs. Federal trust ownership could satisfy the land requirements of the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act.

After administrative review, the Secretary announced approval in 2005 and provided thirty days before acquisition for judicial challenges. Michigan Gambling Opposition sued during that period under environmental and gaming statutes. The Secretary postponed taking title while that case proceeded. The organization lost in the District Court and the D.C. Circuit.

sections.title: A neighbor brings a different challenge
sections.cue: What did Patchak claim, and what interest did he disclaim?
paragraphs: After the D.C. Circuit ruled in the organization’s case, but before the Secretary acquired the land, nearby resident David Patchak filed a separate suit under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Patchak alleged that the Secretary lacked authority to acquire land for this Band because the Band had not been federally recognized when Congress enacted the Indian Reorganization Act in 1934. He alleged that the casino would increase traffic and crime, lower property values, and permanently change the area’s rural character. He sought declaratory and injunctive relief preventing acquisition; he claimed no ownership or other competing interest in the Bradley Property. The Band intervened to defend the Secretary’s decision.

In January 2009, the Supreme Court declined to review Michigan Gambling Opposition’s case, and the Secretary took title. An injunction preventing acquisition was consequently moot, but everyone agreed that Patchak’s continuing suit effectively sought to divest the government of title. The Supreme Court subsequently decided Carcieri, holding that the Secretary’s acquisition authority depended on a tribe’s being under federal jurisdiction in 1934. Whether this Band satisfied that condition—and how federal jurisdiction differed from Patchak’s allegation about formal recognition—remained open.

sections.title: The first courts disagree about who may sue
sections.cue: How did the dispute reach the Supreme Court?
paragraphs: The District Court dismissed Patchak’s suit without deciding whether the acquisition was authorized. It held that his interests fell outside the acquisition statute’s zone of interests. The D.C. Circuit reversed. That court also rejected the Secretary and Band’s alternative argument that sovereign immunity barred the suit.

The Secretary and the Band separately petitioned for Supreme Court review. The Court took both cases to decide those threshold objections. Justice Kagan wrote for eight Justices; Justice Sotomayor dissented.

sections.title: An ownership remedy does not displace every acquisition challenge
sections.cue: Why did the majority hold that federal immunity was waived?
paragraphs: APA §702 generally waived federal sovereign immunity for suits seeking nonmonetary relief against official action, but withheld that waiver where another consent-to-suit statute expressly or impliedly forbade the requested relief. The Secretary and the Band invoked the Quiet Title Act. That statute permitted certain suits involving competing property interests while excluding trust or restricted Indian lands. They argued that Patchak could not use the APA to extinguish the government’s title to land protected by that exclusion.

The majority distinguished the kind of claim from the practical consequence of relief. An adverse owner could not evade the Indian-lands exception by calling a quiet-title suit an APA action. Patchak, however, asserted no competing title: he claimed that the Secretary had exceeded statutory authority, not that the property belonged or should be transferred to him.

The Quiet Title Act’s title, jurisdiction and venue provisions, and pleading requirements supported that distinction. A plaintiff had to identify a personal right, title, or interest in the property. The government’s option to retain land by compensating a successful claimant also fit an ownership dispute; compensating an owner would not answer Patchak’s statutory grievance. Earlier Quiet Title Act decisions likewise involved competing property interests. A detailed statutory remedy could foreclose alternative routes for the same kind of claim, but shared subject matter did not transform Patchak’s different claim into a quiet-title action.

The majority recognized that either kind of lawsuit might disrupt tribal investment. Congress nevertheless had to decide whether to extend the Quiet Title Act’s restrictions to nonclaimants such as Patchak. APA immunity waiver therefore applied here, while the restrictions governing adverse property claimants remained intact.

sections.title: The contemplated casino connects acquisition with neighboring interests
sections.cue: Why could a neighbor invoke a statute intended to help tribes?
paragraphs: The Secretary and Band next argued that the acquisition statute concerned obtaining land, whereas Patchak complained about its eventual use. The majority described the APA zone-of-interests test as relatively undemanding: a plaintiff’s interest need only arguably fall within interests the allegedly violated statute protected or regulated. Congress did not have to intend Patchak as a beneficiary.

Land acquisition under this provision served tribal economic life, and the Secretary considered anticipated uses when deciding whether to acquire property. Department of the Interior regulations required consideration of intended uses and potential land-use conflicts; off-reservation business acquisitions also required a plan describing anticipated benefits. Both the Band’s application and the Secretary’s notice identified a gaming facility. Acquisition and casino development were therefore connected.

Patchak’s alleged economic, environmental, and aesthetic injuries made a foreseeably affected neighbor a reasonable challenger to the statutory limits on that acquisition. His interests fell within the provision’s regulatory scope. This conclusion did not establish that proximity alone satisfied every standing requirement under every statute.

sections.title: Sotomayor focuses on the relief Congress protected against
sections.cue: What did the dissent say the majority’s distinction overlooked?
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor would have dismissed on sovereign-immunity grounds and did not reach standing. She read APA §702’s exception as concerned with forbidden relief: Patchak sought divestiture of Indian trust land, precisely the consequence Congress had restricted through the Quiet Title Act. In her view, that statute’s compensation option, protection of Indian lands, and limits on permissible plaintiffs could not be bypassed by leaving a personal property claim out of the complaint.

Sotomayor also disputed the majority’s narrow conception of quiet title, pointing to the statute’s coverage of lesser interests, including easements and mineral-exploration rights. She feared that property claimants could recruit nonclaimants to pursue the same result, that delayed challenges could destabilize tribal investment, and that disputes over concealed property interests would create pleading incentives and burdens for the government. Those were her objections and predictions, not the Court’s holdings.

sections.title: The suit continues without a ruling against the acquisition
sections.cue: What did the judgment actually accomplish?
paragraphs: The Supreme Court affirmed the D.C. Circuit and remanded for further proceedings. Neither sovereign immunity nor the zone-of-interests requirement barred Patchak’s challenge. The Court did not invalidate the acquisition, order the casino closed, or decide whether the Band had been under federal jurisdiction in 1934. Patchak had won the ability to continue litigating the statutory-authority question, not a decision on its merits.
